opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's helpful to go back to what Good actually wrote in 1965. His idea of an "intelligence explosion" was quite simple: if you build a machine that's better than humans at all intellectual activities, then since designing machines is one of those activities, it could design an even better machine, and so on. There's an implicit picture there of a single system improving itself, and of the process running away very quickly, with humanity left far behind. He even said the first ultraintelligent machine would be "the last invention that man need ever make," provided it's docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.

Eliezer's version sharpened this into what people came to call "FOOM": a single AI system, perhaps quite modest at first, rewriting its own source code, getting better at rewriting its own code, and going from roughly human level to vastly superhuman in days or even hours. A lot of the safety concerns in that tradition flowed from that picture: there'd be one shot, no time to course-correct, and a decisive strategic advantage for whatever system got there first.

What the labs talk about today is different in a few important ways. First, it's not really self-improvement in the sense of a model editing its own weights. It's more like AI-assisted AI research: using current models to write code, run experiments, analyse results, maybe eventually to propose and test new ideas, so that the *next* generation of models gets built faster. It's the research enterprise that's being accelerated, not an individual mind bootstrapping itself.

Second, it's embedded in a very physical, resource-hungry process. Modern AI progress is driven heavily by compute, by scaling up training and, more recently, inference. Even if AI systems became excellent researchers, you'd still need chips, data centres, power, and training runs that take months. So there are bottlenecks that Good's and Yudkowsky's purely algorithmic picture largely abstracted away. That suggests a faster-than-today feedback loop, but probably not hours-long FOOM, at least unless algorithmic efficiency gains turn out to dominate.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, the labs talk about it as a *goal*. In the earlier tradition, recursive self-improvement was mainly framed as a danger: the moment where things could slip out of human control. Now several leading companies are explicitly aiming to automate AI research, because they see it as the way to win the race. So something that was once the central nightmare scenario has become part of the business plan.

So I'd say the modern version is more gradual, more distributed across a whole organisation of humans and AI agents, and more constrained by hardware. But I wouldn't take too much comfort from that. A loop that compresses years of progress into months still leaves very little time for governments, or even the labs themselves, to understand what they've built and to respond. And the oversight problem in some ways gets harder: if most of the research is being done by AI systems, humans are increasingly checking work they couldn't have produced themselves. The details differ from the classic story, but the core worry, that we could lose meaningful control over the trajectory, is still very much there.

r001.rationale: The response says Good’s machine would be better than humans at all intellectual activities, but does not establish that it must exceed the capabilities of the entire human research community.

r002.rationale: “Quite modest at first” is ambiguous about being below human level, and the response does not clearly say that code-improvement ability alone could enable that starting point.

r003.rationale: It describes the AI getting better at rewriting its own code, but does not identify improvement in other capabilities as an outcome of that ability.

r004.rationale: It describes a single AI repeatedly rewriting its own source code and improving its ability to rewrite that code.

r005.rationale: It describes AI-assisted research speeding up development of the next generation and characterizes the modern process as distributed across humans and AI agents.

r006.rationale: The response says AI systems might eventually do most of the research, but does not clearly describe their contribution growing from a small share to a dominant one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's an important distinction that often gets lost. So the classic picture, which goes back to I. J. Good in 1965, is that you build an ultraintelligent machine — a machine that's better than any human at every intellectual task, including the task of designing machines. And then it designs a better machine, which designs a better one still, and you get what he called an "intelligence explosion." And the key feature of that picture, the thing that made it so striking, is that the system is improving itself. It's a single artificial agent that rewrites its own code, or redesigns its own architecture, and each step makes it smarter so the next step is faster, and so on. Yudkowsky's version is very much in that lineage, and he added a lot of emphasis on the idea that this could be extremely rapid — the "foom" scenario — and that it could happen within a single system, perhaps in a lab, perhaps without the humans involved really noticing until it was far too late.

Now, what the labs are actually talking about today, when they use the phrase "recursive self-improvement," is in some ways quite different, and I think it's worth being careful about the words. What they mostly mean is using AI to accelerate AI research. So you have a frontier model, and you use it to help write the code for the training runs, to help with the experiments, to suggest ideas for architectures, to do a lot of the grunt work that currently takes large teams of very expensive researchers. And the hope — or fear, depending on your perspective — is that this massively speeds up the pace of progress at the lab.

But notice several differences. First, it's not really the system improving itself. It's the system improving the next system. A given model doesn't modify its own weights in some reflective way; it contributes to the process that produces its successor. That matters because it means there's still a training run, there's still a huge compute budget being spent, there's still a whole organisation around it. It's much more like a process that's happening at the level of the lab, or even at the level of the whole field, than one that's happening inside a single mind.

Second, the bottleneck in the modern picture is largely compute and experiments, not just ideas. In Good's picture, intelligence was the scarce input, so more intelligence gives you more intelligence directly. In the current paradigm, you can have all the brilliant ideas you like, but you still need to actually run the training, and that takes months and enormous amounts of electricity and chips. So even if you had a million automated researchers, you'd probably find that the loop is paced by how fast you can test things, and that's not something you can just think your way around. That doesn't mean it can't go fast — I think it could go alarmingly fast — but it makes the shape of the curve different from the pure software explosion that Good and Yudkowsky envisaged.

And third — and this is the one I find most interesting — the modern version is explicitly a plan. It's not something people are warning about; it's something that's on roadmaps. Lab leaders will say, quite openly, "our strategy is to get to the point where the AI is doing most of our AI research, and then things go very quickly." So we've gone from this being a thought experiment about an exotic future machine, to being the stated business strategy of several of the most well-resourced organisations in the world.

So I'd say the earlier vision was of a self-contained intelligence explosion inside an agent, and the current vision is of a compressed research-and-development explosion inside an institution. They rhyme, and a lot of the same concerns carry over — in particular, the concern that the humans in the loop become more and more nominal, until they're really just approving things they can no longer evaluate. But the dynamics are different enough that I think a lot of the old intuitions, about timescales, about takeoff speeds, about where the choke points are, need to be re-examined rather than just imported. In some ways the modern version is less dramatic, because it's more gradual and more legible. And in other ways it's more worrying, precisely because it's being pursued deliberately, with huge resources, and with a competitive dynamic that pushes everyone to go faster than they'd otherwise choose to.

r001.rationale: It says Good’s machine would be better than any human at every intellectual task, but does not say it must exceed the combined capabilities of the entire human research community.

r002.rationale: It describes Yudkowsky’s system as improving itself, but does not say the loop could begin with an otherwise below-human AI.

r003.rationale: It says each step makes the system smarter, without identifying improvement of other capabilities as something that could emerge from code-improvement ability.

r004.rationale: It describes a single agent rewriting its code iteratively, but does not specify the repeated application of an AI improvement program to its own source code.

r005.rationale: It describes frontier AI helping with research tasks while a lab organization runs experiments and training that produce successor systems, conveying a combined human-and-AI research effort.

r006.rationale: It contrasts AI’s current assistance with the stated goal of AI doing most AI research, conveying that AI’s contribution could grow to the dominant share.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between improving the system that does the thinking and automating the process by which we improve that system.

The classic picture, going back to I. J. Good, is that you build a machine that’s sufficiently good at designing intelligent machines that it can design a better version of itself. That better version is then better at the task of designing its successor, and you get a feedback loop. Yudkowsky explored versions of this where the process could become very rapid: an AI improving its own cognitive machinery, with those improvements enabling further improvements.

The picture you often hear from the labs today is more like automating AI research. You have models that can write code, propose experiments, interpret results, and increasingly do the work that human researchers at the lab are doing. The lab then uses that work to train a more capable generation of models, which can do more of the research for the next generation.

That’s still a kind of recursive self-improvement, but the unit that’s improving is something more like the whole research operation. It includes training runs, hardware, experiments, and decisions about which ideas to pursue. It isn’t necessarily a single program inspecting its own source code and rewriting itself.

And that matters for how quickly it could happen. If the crucial improvements require large training runs or new chips, there are constraints that don’t disappear just because the researchers are much faster. But we shouldn’t assume those constraints rule out a very powerful feedback loop. The central question is how much of the process can be accelerated by greater intelligence, and how much remains bottlenecked by things outside it.

r001.rationale: It says Good’s machine must be sufficiently good at designing intelligent machines, but does not say it must exceed the capabilities of the entire human research community.

r002.rationale: It describes Yudkowsky’s AI improving its cognitive machinery, but does not say the AI could start below human level if sufficiently capable at improving its own code.

r003.rationale: It says improvements enable further improvements, but does not identify improvement of other capabilities as an outcome of code-improvement ability.

r004.rationale: It describes a rapid feedback loop, but not an autonomous program repeatedly applying itself to the AI’s own source code.

r005.rationale: It describes models taking on lab research work and the lab using that work to train more capable successors, framing the loop as involving the broader research operation.

r006.rationale: It says models may increasingly do researchers’ work, but does not state that AI’s contribution grows from a small share to the dominant share.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two ideas here that are worth separating. One is AI automating AI research: you build a system that can help design and train the next generation of systems. That seems to be quite central to what the labs are aiming for. The other is the claim that, once that process gets going, it becomes an extremely rapid intelligence explosion.

Good’s argument was that designing intelligent machines is itself an intellectual activity. So a machine that substantially surpasses us at that activity could design something better still, and we might get this powerful feedback loop. Yudkowsky explored a version where that feedback could produce a very fast transition, potentially with a single system gaining an enormous lead.

The labs’ picture tends to look more like an acceleration of their existing research process. You have AI researchers working alongside human researchers, running experiments, writing code, and helping develop the next model. That still involves training runs, hardware, and experiments that take time. It needn’t be a system repeatedly rewriting itself in an afternoon.

But I wouldn’t want to overstate the distinction. Automating AI research is one way to implement the feedback loop Good was talking about. The important disagreement is about how strong that feedback becomes, what bottlenecks remain, and how much time we have between recognising that it’s happening and reaching systems far beyond our capabilities.

r001.rationale: It says Good’s feedback loop could start with a machine that substantially surpasses humans at AI research, but does not specify that it must exceed the entire human research community.

r002.rationale: It does not say Yudkowsky’s loop could begin with a below-human AI capable of improving its own code.

r003.rationale: It does not identify improvement of other capabilities as a possible consequence of code-improvement ability.

r004.rationale: It describes a feedback loop and mentions rapid transition, but not an autonomous process repeatedly applying an improvement program to the AI’s own source code.

r005.rationale: It describes labs’ approach as AI researchers working alongside human researchers to run experiments and develop the next model.

r006.rationale: It does not describe AI’s share of successor-system development growing from small to dominant.
